summary: The Thermal equilibrium calculator works out mass (Element 1: The lower temperature one) from the initial temperature, the phase change temperature, the latent heat and the mass. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Thermal equilibrium calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thermal equilibrium calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mass (Element 1: The lower temperature one) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (includes phase change?, the substance (Element 1: The lower temperature one) and the substance & phase change (Element 1: Latent heat)); then you type in the initial temperature (Element 1: The lower temperature one), the phase change temperature (Element 1: Latent heat), the latent heat (Element 1: Latent heat) and the mass (Element 2: The higher temperature one).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Specific heat capacity, opening in joules per kilogram per kelvin
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Energy per mass, opening in kilojoules per kilogram
  • Energy per mass, opening in kilojoules per kilogram
  • Energy, opening in joules

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thermal equilibrium calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial temperature, the phase change temperature and the latent heat — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Thermal equilibrium calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mass (Element 1: The lower temperature one), derived from the initial temperature, the phase change temperature and the latent heat. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thermal equilibrium calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial temperature, the phase change temperature, the latent heat and the mass, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter heat transferred (Element 1: The lower temperature one) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Heat transferred (Element 1: The lower temperature one) opens in joules and the chip beside it offers 33 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Specific heat capacity = 0 J/(kg·K). Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thermal equilibrium calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
